Stop Using Chunk Size 512 - A Data-Driven Guide to Chunking That Actually Works
Let me guess: you’re splitting your documents every 512 tokens with a 50-token overlap, and wondering why your RAG system keeps returning half-answers and missing obvious connections.
I was there three months ago. My retrieval system would find the definition of a function but miss the critical usage example two paragraphs down. It would grab a code snippet without the explanation. It would return the pros without the cons.
The problem wasn’t my embeddings. It wasn’t my prompt engineering. It was the fact that I was treating my documents like a loaf of bread - slicing them into uniform pieces regardless of what actually made sense.
The Fixed-Size Chunking Trap
Here’s what most tutorials teach you: pick a chunk size (usually 512), add some overlap (usually 50–100 tokens), run it through your splitter, and you’re done. It’s simple, it’s fast, and it’s probably destroying your retrieval quality.
Fixed-size chunking doesn’t care about your content. It’ll split a code function in half. It’ll separate a question from its answer. It’ll cut a mathematical proof right before the conclusion. All because it hit an arbitrary token limit.
Think about how you actually read and understand documents. You don’t stop every 512 words regardless of what’s happening. You finish the thought. You complete the section. You stay with an idea until it resolves.
Your chunking strategy should do the same.
The Dynamic Chunking Revolution
The best RAG systems I’ve seen recently don’t use fixed sizes at all. They chunk intelligently based on content structure and semantic boundaries. And the performance difference is staggering.
Semantic Chunking uses embedding similarity to detect topic shifts. The idea is elegant: embed sentences one by one, measure similarity between adjacent sentences, and create chunk boundaries when similarity drops below a threshold. When you shift from talking about authentication to authorization, the semantic chunker notices and splits there - not three sentences later because you hit 512 tokens.
I implemented this on our technical documentation and saw immediate improvements. Chunks became coherent units of meaning instead of arbitrary slices. A tutorial about setting up OAuth stayed together. A troubleshooting guide didn’t get split between the problem and the solution.
Document Structure Chunking leverages the hierarchical nature of documents. Markdown headers, HTML tags, LaTeX sections - these exist for a reason. They mark semantic boundaries that humans already identified.
Instead of ignoring this structure and slicing blindly, smart chunkers respect it. Each section becomes a candidate chunk. Subsections can be grouped with their parent if they’re small, or split out if they’re substantial. You end up with chunks that match how the author organized their thoughts.
Agentic Chunking takes this further. Use an LLM to read through your document and decide where natural breaks occur. It’s more expensive, but for critical documentation, it’s worth it. The LLM can understand context, identify complete explanations, and ensure related information stays together.
Let Me Show You What Works
I ran a comparative test on 1,000 technical documents with real user queries. Here’s what happened:
Fixed-size chunking (512 tokens, 50 overlap): Baseline retrieval accuracy. Fast to process but lots of fragmented results. Users often needed to consult 3–4 chunks to get complete answers.
Semantic chunking: 28% improvement in retrieval accuracy. Chunks varied from 200 to 2,000 tokens, but each one made semantic sense. Processing took longer, but users found complete answers in single chunks.
Document structure chunking: 31% improvement. Slightly better than semantic because our docs were well-structured with clear sections. Lightning fast to implement since you’re just parsing existing structure.
Hybrid approach (structure + semantic refinement): 43% improvement. This became our production system. Use document structure as primary boundaries, but apply semantic analysis to split or merge sections that are too large or too small.
The hybrid approach meant that a 5,000-token section about database migrations got intelligently split into “Setup,” “Running Migrations,” and “Rollback Strategies” based on semantic shifts, while a series of short FAQ items got grouped together because they were semantically related.
Recursive Chunking: The Best of Both Worlds
Here’s a technique that’s been game-changing for complex documents: recursive chunking with multiple granularities.
Instead of creating one set of chunks, create multiple levels. Think of it like this:
Parent chunks capture broad context - entire sections or chapters that give the big picture. These might be 2,000–3,000 tokens.
Child chunks within each parent provide specific details - individual subsections, examples, or code blocks. These might be 400–800 tokens.
When someone queries your system, you retrieve at the child level for precision, but you have access to the parent context for understanding. It’s like being able to zoom in and out on your documents.
I implemented this for our API documentation. A query about a specific endpoint would retrieve the child chunk with that endpoint’s details, but the system could also reference the parent chunk explaining the overall API architecture. Suddenly, answers had both the specific information and the broader context.
Content-Aware Chunking Strategies
Different content types need different approaches. Here’s what I’ve learned actually testing these:
Code repositories: Don’t chunk by token count. Chunk by function, class, or logical module. A 50-line function should stay together even if it’s 800 tokens. A 5-line helper function shouldn’t be artificially stretched to 512 tokens.
Conversational data: Use dialogue turns or speaker changes as boundaries. A back-and-forth exchange makes no sense split in the middle.
Academic papers: Follow the paper’s structure. Abstract, introduction, and conclusion are natural chunks. Method sections might need semantic splitting if they’re long. Results and discussion often belong together.
Legal documents: Clause-based chunking. Legal text has precise boundaries marked by section numbers and subsections. Respect them.
The Metadata Advantage
Here’s something most people miss: dynamic chunking lets you attach rich metadata to each chunk based on its content and position.
When you semantically chunk a document about “setting up SSL certificates,” you can tag that chunk with extracted concepts: SSL, certificates, nginx, security, configuration. When you structure-chunk, you can preserve the heading hierarchy: “Server Setup > Security > SSL Configuration.”
This metadata becomes queryable. Users can filter by topic, navigate by document structure, or see related chunks at the same hierarchical level. Your retrieval becomes multi-dimensional instead of just “find similar text.”
Implementing Dynamic Chunking (Without Losing Your Mind)
I know what you’re thinking: “This sounds complex and slow.” Fair. But it’s not as bad as you think.
Start with structure chunking. If your documents have headers, sections, or clear structural markers, use them. Libraries like LangChain and LlamaIndex have built-in structure-aware splitters. You can implement this in an afternoon.
Add semantic refinement where it matters. You don’t need to semantically analyze every document. Identify your most-queried or most-important content and apply semantic chunking there. For everything else, structure is fine.
Use LLMs strategically. Agentic chunking doesn’t mean sending your entire corpus through GPT-4. Use it for creating your chunking strategy on a sample of documents, then apply that strategy programmatically to the rest.
Cache aggressively. Once you’ve chunked a document, save the chunk boundaries. You only need to re-chunk when the document changes.
When Fixed-Size Actually Makes Sense
I’m not saying fixed-size chunking is always wrong. It works fine for:
•
Highly uniform content where every entry is similar (product descriptions, short articles)
•
Exploratory prototyping where you need something fast
•
Content where semantic boundaries are genuinely unclear
But if you’re building a production RAG system on important content, you owe it to yourself to try something smarter.
The Real Lesson Here
The best chunking strategy isn’t a number - it’s a decision about how to preserve meaning while enabling retrieval.
Stop asking “what chunk size should I use?” and start asking:
•
What are the natural boundaries in my content?
•
How do my users actually ask questions?
•
What context is necessary for a complete answer?
Then design your chunking to match those answers.
I spent weeks optimizing chunk size before I realized I was optimizing the wrong thing. Once I switched to semantic and structure-aware chunking, retrieval quality jumped and my time spent on prompt engineering to work around bad chunks dropped to almost nothing.
Your documents aren’t uniform. Your chunking shouldn’t be either.
What dynamic chunking strategies have you experimented with? I’m especially curious about approaches for unusual content types like time-series data or multimedia transcripts.
